==Problem==

How many positive integers can fill the blank in the sentence below?

“One positive integer is _____ more than twice another, and the sum of the two numbers is <imath>28</imath>.”

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 6 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 7 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 8 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 9 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 10</imath>

==Solution==

Let <imath>m</imath> and <imath>n</imath> be positive integers such that <imath>m>n</imath> and <imath>m+n=28.</imath> It follows that <imath>m=2n+d</imath> for some positive integer <imath>d.</imath> We wish to find the number of possible values for <imath>d.</imath>

By substitution, we have <imath>(2n+d)+n=28,</imath> from which <imath>d=28-3n.</imath> Note that <imath>n=1,2,3,\ldots,9</imath> each generate a positive integer for <imath>d,</imath> so there are <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 9}</imath> possible values for <imath>d.</imath>

~MRENTHUSIASM

==Solution 2==
Let the positive integer be <imath>x</imath>, ____ be <imath>z</imath> and twice another <imath>2y</imath>. We can form the following equations:

<imath>x</imath> + <imath>y</imath> = <imath>28</imath>

<imath>x</imath> - <imath>2y</imath> = <imath>z</imath>

We use elimination to get this equation:
<imath>3y</imath> = 28 - <imath>z</imath>. The smallest that <imath>z</imath> can be is <imath>1</imath> (<imath>28</imath> - <imath>1</imath> = <imath>27</imath> ✓), and the largest <imath>25</imath> (<imath>28</imath> - <imath>25</imath> = <imath>3</imath> ✓). <imath>25</imath> - <imath>1</imath> = 24, and since we only want multiples of <imath>3</imath> this will occur every 3 numbers. 24 / 3 = 8. We are missing the <imath>1</imath> which we subtracted earlier, so our final answer will be 9 numbers, or <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 9}</imath>. 

~OddPeppyBoots
